evidence.exact_quote: The canonical human-in-the-loop contract remains a blocked-runtime overlay.

items.impact: Establishes one runtime-native approval identity and action model for all HITL consumers.
items.statement: The prologue makes blocked episodes, ordered runtime actions, package/seam gates, replayable events, and explicit compatibility retirement the canonical HITL model.
items.title: Blocked-runtime HITL model is canonical

evidence.exact_quote: Runtime HITL persistence is keyed by blocked episode identity first. `checkpoints.hitl.{run_id}` and `checkpoints.hitl` are compatibility paths only; `/runtime/storage` records must distinguish concurrent pending-HITL episodes in the same run by `run_id`, `node_id`, `blocked_sequence`, `attempt_id?`, `approval_scope_key`, actor/account/lane context, and approver identity. The event family must support a three-way join among the blocked episode, approval-identity record, and tool-level or /tool-definition request that triggered the wait.

items.impact: Two surfaces can resolve the same episode, or approval can race with abort, expiry, restart, or stale projection, without a defined winner, idempotency key, rejection result, or rollback rule.
items.statement: The source requires identity separation and freshness binding but does not define atomic compare-and-set semantics, duplicate-command idempotency, event ordering, or user-visible conflict outcomes for concurrent resolution commands.
items.title: Concurrent blocked-episode resolution lacks an atomicity contract

evidence.exact_quote: HITL is the approval consumer for shared-runtime, multi-lane execution. Assistant chat, validation-pass output, wizard-handoff payloads, DAE side-effect interception, and tool-event records must preserve `effective_account_id`, `requested_account`, `requested_account_id`, `execution_role`, permission posture, actor identity, lane identity, and `attempt_id` so a later reviewer can tell who asked, who approved, under which `/account/role`, on which `/package/lane/attempt`, and whether an `/always` policy was scoped safely. Any rewrite-alignment or post-hoc explanation that omits these fields is under-attributed and lane-unsafe.

items.impact: Durable multi-actor and account provenance can expose sensitive identities or outlive its purpose without clear read authority, redaction, retention, export, and deletion rules.
items.statement: The plan requires extensive durable attribution but does not specify minimization, encryption, access control, retention, redaction, deletion, or support-export handling for approval provenance.
items.title: Approval provenance has no privacy lifecycle

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: The canonical HITL contract remains a blocked-runtime overlay with run_id, node_id, blocked_sequence, optional attempt_id, blocked_reason_code, ordered allowed_action_ids, approval_scope_key, optional detail_ref, and optional approver_identity; blocked_sequence is the canonical approval anchor and action_available rows derive from the same blocked-runtime action set.

items.impact: Provides addressable PlanUnits for document authority, replayable events, request fields, attribution, persistence, and compatibility separation.
items.statement: HITL-002 through HITL-007 convert the prologue into explicit owner, event, request, provenance, persistence, and compatibility contracts.
items.title: Core HITL authority and identity PlanUnits are explicit

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Runtime HITL persistence is keyed by blocked episode identity first; checkpoints.hitl.{run_id} and checkpoints.hitl are compatibility paths only, and runtime storage must distinguish concurrent pending HITL episodes by run_id, node_id, blocked_sequence, optional attempt_id, approval_scope_key, actor/account/lane context, and approver identity while supporting a three-way join among the blocked episode, approval identity record, and triggering tool request.

items.impact: Partial persistence of the episode, identity record, or triggering request can produce an unresolvable approval or an audit record that cannot prove its authority.
items.statement: HITL-006 requires a three-way join but does not define transaction boundaries, orphan repair, uniqueness constraints, startup reconciliation, or acceptance oracles for partially written join participants.
items.title: Three-way approval join lacks consistency and repair semantics

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: The historical HITLRequest request-era contract is a compatibility bridge subordinate to the runtime blocked episode; request_id, tier_id, tier_type, request_kind=tier_boundary_approval, allowed_actions, allowed_actions[], tier/request_kind/allowed_actions, and hitl.approval_requested must not become a second action family, and HITL classification keeps source, request, and execution/result axes separate.

items.impact: Legacy producers or consumers may silently preserve a second action ontology indefinitely or fail ambiguously when aliases disappear.
items.statement: The compatibility bridge names retired fields but has no version negotiation, telemetry, deprecation deadline, rejection behavior, or migration oracle proving every caller resolves through blocked_sequence.
items.title: Request-era bridge has no measurable retirement path

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Clarification questions and blocked-resolution flows use node-effective execution metadata, palette-friendly copy, and detail pivots without losing runtime truth; UI and storage routes must not cross-wire governance approvals with tool approvals, and hitl.* event rows carry config, run.started, usage.event, actor projections, meta links, action-family normalization, and current blocked-episode mutation binding.

items.impact: Defines automation-first boundaries, truthful surface routing, runtime-native shims, normalized recovery labels, narrow tray behavior, and debug grant scope.
items.statement: HITL-008 through HITL-013 cover boundary unification, execution metadata, event-to-surface routing, compatibility shims, transition reports, tray/correlation rules, and bounded debug grants.
items.title: Boundary, surface, and debug-grant semantics are addressable

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Debug Mode may request a run-scoped front-door grant for repeated low-risk investigation actions, but the grant remains represented through the canonical blocked-runtime overlay, is anchored by the blocked episode and investigation identity, does not create a separate approval transport, preserves degraded/blocked continuation when declined, limits scope to low-risk evidence reads and declared temporary instrumentation, and is revoked on grant revocation or investigation finish.

items.impact: A crashed, disconnected, or long-running investigation may retain temporary instrumentation authority or leave ambiguous cleanup and degraded-state recovery.
items.statement: The grant is bounded by purpose and revocation but lacks an expiry, action budget, restart behavior, disconnect behavior, atomic revocation rule, cleanup receipt, and oracle proving temporary instrumentation was removed.
items.title: Debug front-door grant lacks crash-safe lifecycle controls

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Consequential approval and recovery transitions use a shared transition report with from/to state, target object, actor/source, reason, prerequisite evidence, review or corroboration references, and downstream obligations; recovery labels distinguish true Undo from Restore, Rollback, Retry from Safe Point, Reopen, Start fresh attempt, and compensating_action_only behavior.

items.impact: Dense state reports and action distinctions may be inaccessible to keyboard, screen-reader, low-vision, or non-English users and may be mistranslated into misleading recovery promises.
items.statement: The visible recovery vocabulary is exacting, but the PlanUnit provides no accessible-name, focus order, announcement, non-color state, localization-key, terminology-lock, or text-expansion acceptance criteria.
items.title: Recovery reports have no accessibility or localization contract

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: HITL is configured in the GUI and persisted in one canonical execution-affecting config block shaped as hitl.phase, hitl.task, and hitl.subtask; the structure lives inside GuiConfig, persists in redb at config:gui.hitl, GUI controls read and write the exact structure, Option B runtime config construction copies it unchanged into the run snapshot at run start, and no second backend-only HITL key family exists.

items.impact: Defines optional autonomy-safe UX, canonical gates, one persisted config, blocked-episode pauses, and runtime-derived controls.
items.statement: HITL-014 through HITL-020 define optional autonomy behavior, derived grouping, package/seam gates, independent toggles, GUI persistence, pause integration, and runtime control labels.
items.title: Optional UX, gate, config, and action contracts are explicit

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: HITL is configured in the GUI and persisted in one canonical execution-affecting config block shaped as hitl.phase, hitl.task, and hitl.subtask; the structure lives inside GuiConfig, persists in redb at config:gui.hitl, GUI controls read and write the exact structure, Option B runtime config construction copies it unchanged into the run snapshot at run start, and no second backend-only HITL key family exists.

items.impact: Concurrent GUI writes, failed persistence, schema upgrades, or run-start races can make displayed toggles disagree with the durable config or captured run snapshot.
items.statement: The exact config shape and copy point are fixed, but revisioning, compare-and-set behavior, durable-write acknowledgement, migration defaults, corruption recovery, and the linearization point between edits and run snapshot creation are absent.
items.title: HITL config lacks versioning and run-start race semantics

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: HITL exposes three independent user-facing grouping toggles for phase, task, and subtask, all defaulting off; toggles request approval at the corresponding package/seam gate decision point before the next grouping begins and must not redefine approval_scope_key, blocked identity, recovery semantics, persistence ownership, or package/seam gate ownership.

items.impact: Different implementations may pause at different package or seam decisions for the same phase/task/subtask setting, producing unexpected extra, missing, or duplicate approvals.
items.statement: The source refers to the corresponding package/seam gate but does not define the mapping algorithm, precedence when multiple toggles match one gate, deduplication, or behavior when grouping boundaries and graph gates do not align one-to-one.
items.title: Phase/task/subtask toggles lack deterministic gate mapping

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Canonical blocked classification uses concern_reason with optional detail_ref for additional structured metadata; ordered allowed_action_ids is the only canonical action enumeration for Runtime, Dashboard, Assistant, and APIs; canonical approval resolution uses approval_outcome and approval_recorded_at scoped by approval_scope_key, and durable approver_identity records who approved or declined.

items.impact: Connects Dashboard and Assistant UX to one blocked identity, one config, durable recovery, retired tier payloads, and canonical approval outcomes.
items.statement: HITL-021 through HITL-027 define CtA addressability, pause separation, implementation hooks, restart correlation, tier retirement, canonical resolution fields, and recovery attachment.
items.title: Dashboard, persistence, and recovery identity are unified

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: When Orchestrator pauses for HITL, Dashboard surfaces the state as a warning or Call to Action, and HITL prompts are addressable through the chat Assistant or direct Dashboard controls while remaining a single concept owned by Dashboard warning/CtA and Assistant integration.

canonical_text: Implementation planning hooks require shared runtime config for approval/blocking policy, transition into canonical blocked episode flow rather than tier-local pause flags, persistence and restore of the same blocked episode so restart, retry, skip, abort, and recovery actions stay attached to original runtime identity, and Dashboard/Assistant surfacing without rewriting identity or action set.

items.impact: Assistant and direct controls can submit conflicting or duplicate destructive resolutions, while stale surfaces may continue presenting an already-consumed action set.
items.statement: Cross-surface addressability is specified, but command deduplication, stale-action disablement, conflict results, optimistic UI rollback, offline submission, and reconciliation after one surface wins are not.
items.title: Dashboard and Assistant can race to resolve one episode

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Acceptance carry-through transfers execution_role, requested_account_id, operational_identity, account switch and pressure ownership, blocked_sequence minting, startup recovery handshake, and DAE jail/approval policy into owner and consumer docs; approval_scope_key is the durable blocked-episode scope key across actor, lane, run, node, and account context, reused across permissions, HITL, doom-loop handling, and session approval caching, while provider-native correlation lives in dedicated fields and approver identity persists durably.

items.impact: Reusing one durable scope key across permissions, HITL, doom-loop, and session caches can create correlation and privilege bleed if visibility, cache partitioning, and lifecycle differ.
items.statement: The durable key's reuse is required, but namespace partitioning, least-privilege readers, rotation, retention, redaction, cache eviction, and prevention of cross-account/session correlation are not defined.
items.title: Approval scope reuse lacks privacy and isolation controls

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: 'HITL approval/rejection resolution is a primary scheduler wake trigger: hitl.approved and hitl.rejected cause immediate queue reevaluation while unrelated runnable work continues; approval waits consume the shared temporal taxonomy as approval_wait and possibly long_governance_wait, known timers must not render generic deadlock/stall or auto-pause unrelated runnable work, and user_visible_wait_timer_expiry keeps the same blocked episode identity.'

items.impact: Defines scheduling wakeups, wait classification, explicit rerun/skip/abort semantics, canonical recovery actions and labels, plus shared permission-ladder consumption.
items.statement: HITL-028 through HITL-034 standardize scheduler wake, waits, recovery paths, action gating, visible labels, and shared approval-ladder consumption.
items.title: Wait, recovery, and permission contracts are addressable

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: 'HITL approval/rejection resolution is a primary scheduler wake trigger: hitl.approved and hitl.rejected cause immediate queue reevaluation while unrelated runnable work continues; approval waits consume the shared temporal taxonomy as approval_wait and possibly long_governance_wait, known timers must not render generic deadlock/stall or auto-pause unrelated runnable work, and user_visible_wait_timer_expiry keeps the same blocked episode identity.'

items.impact: An approval arriving at the countdown boundary can race expiry, restart recovery, or scheduler wake and create double transitions, lost approval, or inconsistent UI and queue state.
items.statement: The timer taxonomy and retained identity are explicit, but authoritative clock, deadline inclusivity, cancellation, event ordering, exactly-once scheduler wake, restart catch-up, and approval-versus-expiry winner rules are absent.
items.title: Approval expiry can race resolution and scheduler wake

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: HITL-specific affordances consume the shared permission ladder instead of defining a shorter local approval menu; approval choices are deny, once, for session, and always, batch web review may present one domain-grouped approval surface, question defaults to allow only when HITL is available and otherwise remains ask-gated, and HITL surfaces do not create a competing approval vocabulary.

items.impact: Surfaces can conflate permission scope choices with runtime resolution actions, incorrectly interpret deny versus decline, or expose always beyond the intended account/lane/tool scope.
items.statement: The plan defines runtime action families and a separate shared permission ladder but does not define their typed composition, label mapping, allowed combinations, scope-key derivation, or the precise meaning and security preconditions of HITL availability for question defaulting.
items.title: Permission scopes and runtime actions lack a typed mapping

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: HITL surfaces use canonical visible labels Approve, Decline, Retry from safe point, Start fresh attempt, Resume after prerequisite, Replan, Skip node, and Abort run; Reject, Deny, and other variants map back to canonical action families, and after decline/reject the surface chooses among safe-point retry, fresh attempt, Replan, Skip node only when permitted, or debug verification rerun in the active isolated automation session unless corrupted state requires a fresh isolated session.

items.impact: Users may choose a destructive or irreversible action from ambiguous focus, truncated translations, inaccessible status changes, or localized labels that break canonical action-family mapping.
items.statement: Canonical labels and enablement are defined, but destructive-action confirmation, keyboard/focus behavior, screen-reader announcements, disabled-reason exposure, localization keys, text expansion, and locale-safe alias mapping have no acceptance oracles.
items.title: Canonical action labels lack accessible and localized interaction rules

segments.summary: Reviewed the complete prologue for canonical blocked-runtime behavior, event replay, provenance, storage, gate, UI, recovery, debug-grant, settings, and adversarial lifecycle/race gaps.
Reviewed shared approval-ladder continuation and HITL-002 through HITL-007 for authority, event, request, provenance, persistence, compatibility, join-repair, and retirement completeness.
Reviewed HITL-008 through HITL-013 for boundary, routing, compatibility, recovery labels, tray/correlation, debug grants, and adversarial lifecycle and accessible-display behavior.
Reviewed HITL-014 through HITL-020 for optional autonomy, grouping/gate behavior, config persistence, run snapshots, pause actions, and adversarial mapping and write-race gaps.

Reviewed HITL-021 through HITL-027 for Dashboard/Assistant addressability, pause separation, persistence, recovery identity, tier retirement, action derivation, and adversarial cross-surface and privacy isolation gaps.

Reviewed HITL-028 through HITL-034 for scheduler wake, wait timers, rerun/skip/abort, action families, gating, labels, permission-ladder consumption, and adversarial timer, mapping, accessibility, and localization gaps.
